Examining PC game trends: beyond the Steam tag!
Here’s another way to look at emerging trends. Also: GameDiscoverCo Show & lots of discovery news
Simon Carless
Nov 18, 2026
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
As November is part-way through (how did that happen?), the newsletter’s back. And this time, we’re using proprietary analysis to try to group Steam game trends into handy buckets. (Because if there’s anything that’s cutting-edge and high tech in 2026, it’s… buckets.)
Before we start, the Boss Fight Books folks do super-fun critical analysis books (Derek Yu’s analysis of his own game, Spelunky is ‘free’ for GDCo Basic/Pro subs !), and its latest Kickstarter is for Gabe Durham’s ‘But Can It Run Doom?’ , about “How tinkerers got DOOM running on: consoles, lamps, pregnancy tests [and] DNA.” Oh yes.
[ NEED THE BEST DATA? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP server, by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Basic gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more .]
Game disco news: spot the Steam capsule fails?
And let’s start out with a little game platform & discovery shenanigans, a little bit like this:
As we posted on LinkedIn : “Steam's been kind enough to allow 'artwork over-rides' on Steam capsule images for DLC/updates… but a lot of games are doing the wrong things, apparently!” Above are Valve’s new spoof-y examples from its Artwork Overrides page on what NOT to do - can you spot what’s wrong in all 3? (Answers on Fri!)
GTA VI tidbits: the game’s preloading is causing major download traffic spikes in Europe , as I was quoted in GI.biz noting the pre-load for Black Myth Wukong on Steam in 2024 spiked Steam bandwidth usage up >3x; the least conventional way to play GTA VI on launch is via cloud streaming onto your Xbox One .
Looking at GDCo’s trending unreleased Steam games by new wishlists , week ending Nov. 16th, survival strategy game Ebbtide is back to #1, with Deadlock & Soulframe at #2 and #4. And slick looking co-op PvE shooter Exterminauts boosted up to #5, due to a beta.
Further down the chart, past the just-releasing traffic sim Trafficity & first-person dungeon autobattler Dungeonbound ? Some titles we’ve never talked about at all, including multiplayer road digging sim Dirt Town (#8) and first-person fantasy exploration game with elaborate spells Aveltuner (#9) .
The latest Twitch platform announcements from TwitchCon San Diego included Stream Recaps (easier highlight reels), simpler clipping, and multiple integrations with Luna - “streamers can invite up to seven viewers to join them in supported Amazon Luna GameNight titles” & a ‘Play On Luna” button beneath Twitch streams.
Wondering what Steam’s doing for Black Friday? Well, wonder no more - they’re repeating last year’s ‘unofficial official sale’ treatment from Nov 26-30, “giving the Discounts & Events page the Black Friday treatment… Please do keep in mind that just like last year, this period is not exempt from discount cooldowns.” (So: some better algo featuring, since there’ll be no curated deals then, but not a giant push…)
Infinite kudos to Chris Zukowski for his summary of when devs should be worried about AI/’ fast follow’ clones : “1. Built upon a… ‘gimmick’; 2. Art is not a differentiating feature. 3. Design is [predictable with a genre]; 4. Content is ‘systematic’ not hand crafted.” (He’s not saying don’t make these, just they are more clone-able.)
When is a door not a door? When it’s ajar. This type of statement feels like the latest positioning from Xbox’s Jason Ronald on the upcoming Helix device: “Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games.” (I think I know what he means, but…)
Streamer things: go browse the winners of The Streamer Awards 2026 and check out some of their VOD videos, for vibes context; Hatchet thinks TikTok Live is the fastest growing platform in game streaming , measuring 2.5b hours in H1 2026 (level with Kick, and behind Twitch at 9.1b & YouTube Gaming at 4.0b.)
VR things: Meta “may soon rebrand Horizon+, its VR game subscription service for Quest, to ‘Meta VR+ ’, as [it’s] bundling a number of 3D films to better appeal to Meta VR Glasses owners” ; Meta says in-app purchases have now surpassed paid app sales as the largest source of revenue on Quest's Meta Horizon store (from Jan-Sep 2026).
Microlinks: physical media’s dead? Ocarina Of Time just sold 1m physical copies in the U.S. in a week , says Circana; the AI-aided QSSR upscaling is coming to more PS5 games , inc. Spider-Man 2, No Man’s Sky & Arc Raiders; Itch.io is adding support for Flash games via the open-source Ruffle emulator, bless them.

PC game trends: beyond the humble Steam tag…
Problem: there’s so many darn games on Steam nowadays that it’s difficult to work out trends. Possible solution: Steam tags? Up to 20 are assigned per game from a master list. That’s what most people try to use, to categorize what’s happening with games on Steam, since they are a) universal and b) both devs and players contribute to them.
But there’s an issue with this solution: though Steam did add ~25 tags in May 2026 , including some new subgenres (Cleaning, Desktop Companion, Incremental) , tags are not intended to encapsulate every new game micro-trend, and are arguably shouldn’t. (Only 8 tags were added from 2023-2025 - not designed to be an evolving record.)
And while GameDiscoverCo uses tags extensively in our data and they’re very helpful, we need to go beyond that. So we’ve devised a new ‘Trends’ taxonomy for Steam games to group 1,400 separate trends (and overarching categories for some of ‘em), with between 3 and 73 ‘notable games’ in each.
The hottest 8 are shown above in a screenshot from this new GameDiscoverCo Pro feature. Immediate disclaimer - this is absolutely a subjective ‘ask computer to find new trends using lots of criteria’ exercise which is mushy around the edges. But we also found a lot of interesting stuff. Notes on the ‘hottest*’ GDCo Trends above:
Checkpoint inspection sims? People really love this mechanic: Papers, Please (2013!) eventually birthed a new set of 3D job sim inspection simulators like Contraband Police & Quarantine Zone, as well as creepypasta spinoffs like No, I’m Not A Human. (Upcoming: Totally Secure Airport, Gate Guard Simulator.)
‘Car survival’ is #2 and perhaps under-discussed as a trend: described as “drive through dangerous areas, scavenge supplies and parts, and keep a vehicle repaired and upgraded to continue exploring”, this encompasses everything from Pacific Drive and Drive Beyond Horizons to Funnel Runners.
The rest of the Top 8 are pretty eclectic, but we recognize ‘em: on the bigger-budget side, PvPvE Extraction Shooters & the related Tarkov-Inspired Extraction Shooters get in at #3 and #4, with Monster Taming RPGs, Hazardous Delivery (cargo delivering!), Repair Shop Simulators & Creature Evolution Survival (recent hits Voidling Bound & Everything Is Crab) round things out.
(*For ‘hottest’, we’re looking at a combination of recent successes in the past year, with upcoming games with high wishlist counts. So it’s about what Steam says it likes, recently!)
Just to show you what the details pages for each of these trends look like, here’s one for ‘Checkpoint Inspection Sims’ so you can, uhh, inspect the specifics:
Since there are 1,400 trends in GDCo’s Trends set, it’s spectacularly difficult to summarize in one short text newsletter. But we did try to make some kind of ‘meta-scaffolding’ for the trends, in the form of trend categories.
About 400 of these trends have those, and here’s a screenshot of the top of the (very long) page looking at all of these grouped categories for trends:
Now we admit, if you squint there’s likely some semi-duplicative trends in here (Zombie Horde Nights vs. Zombie Wave Survival, anyone?) But the algorithm has found them because there’s a lot of intense competition there. So we still find this type of grouping helpful.
There’s a lot of intensity in Vampire Survivors-likes (#1), and we’re not surprised to see Job Sims at #2. And heck, #3 is Shop Slop, which is a subcategory of job sim…(BTW, did you know that Parryslop and Sortslop are also slop microgenres now, the first name more tongue-in-cheek than the second?)
Anyhow, here’s all of the trend categories with at least 5 trends associated with them:
Most are fairly self-explanatory, but I did have to look up a couple: Movement encompasses parkour-like platformers, skateboarding, and 3D grappling hook games, and Environmental Puzzles includes gravity & portal puzzles and ‘awkward task simulators’ like Octodad and Job Simulator.
So here’s some trends. And here’s the most important question of all: should you run towards or away from these trends ? Because trends are crowded, right? The answer is: I’m not sure! Many of these trends have a low barrier to entry, and we have some game analyses coming up from successful titles who very much ‘paved their own road’.
But I think there’s value in understanding trends, because some of these elements can be used in games, even if you’re not squarely in the core trend space. (For example: anomaly hunting can be applied to various subgenres, as can delivery mechanics.) So: ‘lots of inspiration, not so much direct cloning’ might be the prescription for success?
GameDiscoverCo Show: ‘$500m’ = how much?
We bounce right back again with the newest GameDiscover Show , ft. myself (Simon) and Post Games’ Chris Plante discussing the latest. Reminder: sub to the podcast via Apple Podcasts , Spotify & elsewhere (audio), with a video version on YouTube (above).
The latest GDCo Show examines what a budget of ‘$500 million’ r eally means, and whether order of magnitude is the bigger issue than specific sums. Also: game biz objections to Europe’s Digital Fairness Act, data brokers pursuing game source code purchases for AI training, and the latest PC game launcher security issues.

How PlayStation became the home of Grand Theft Auto
We’re joined by Kelly Sumner, Chris Deering, Shuhei Yoshida, Shawn Layden and Peter Moore to look back on the history of GTA
Christopher Dring
Nov 18
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
How Sony secured GTA 3
Xbox’s GTA 4 fight back
How GTA changed Sony’s studios
GTA 3’s unspent $600,000 music budget
Plus, GTA 6 predictions, and more stories
Hello there!
We’re out a day earlier this week for Rockstar-related reasons. And we have a fun special edition of the Show today.
The launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is an entertainment event like nothing this industry has seen before. Movies have their Star Wars moments, music have had their major album launches, and I remember Harry Potter mania vividly. But games? I think this might be a first.
GTA is about more than numbers. But we’re The Game Business, and so we’ll be watching to see if it can hit that $2 billion figure in one weekend. It’d be a remarkable feat. And I’ll be fascinated to see what happens for the artists, actors and locations that are featured within the game.
But that’s all to come. For today, I’ve decided to look back at the business history of GTA. And we have some big names sharing their insight, memories and stories from working on the business-side of GTA. We’ve got former PlayStation execs Chris Deering, Shuhei Yoshida and Shawn Layden , plus ex-Take-Two CEO Kelly Sumner and Xbox 360 boss Peter Moore . It’s a bumper edition. And you can listen to the whole thing above, or check out some of the key highlights below.
Enjoy!
PlayStation US didn’t want GTA
The exclusivity deal that brought Grand Theft Auto 3, Vice City and San Andreas to PlayStation began at E3 in Los Angeles.
“We stayed at the Sunset Marquis Hotel, which is a hotel where the British people stay,” said former PlayStation European boss Chris Deering. “The PS2 was coming, and we were thinking, ‘Well, we’re here at E3, we can make contact with major publishers and see if there’s anything we can do on exclusivity.’ Because we knew the Xbox was coming.
“We had a little meeting room. And we were visited by Kelly Sumner, who was head of Take-Two at the time.”
Deering already had his eye on a game. Before travelling to E3, he received a tip off from one of his internal third-party relations staff.
“I walked by the office and said, “Anything coming down this pipeline that’s interesting?” And someone said, ‘Well, there’s this new GTA.’ I said, ‘GTA?’ ‘Yeah. It’s really good.’
“Kelly was not the first that came through the door, but I remember it was at the end of the day. So, we didn’t have a lot of time, and he had two titles. The first one was something called State of Emergency. We took both.”
Sumner remembered: “Sony came to us and said that we were looking for a product to become exclusive, because they wanted to fend off Microsoft.
“The whole of Take-Two and Rockstar were massively supportive of PlayStation, and not massively supportive of Xbox at the time. We really weren’t sure whether [Xbox] was going to do anything. So, we were very happy to do an exclusive, but not only that, they gave us a substantial amount of cash, and for us that was pretty important. But even more important, as it turned out, was they gave us a discount on the production costs.”
Both Deering and Sumner estimates that Sony gave them between $2.50 - $3 off per unit, and so the deal was worth “tens and tens and tens of millions of dollars” for Take-Two.
Deering continued: “I said, ‘Can we do two or three in a row?’ Because I knew they’d be another one. And it was a jovial meeting. I don’t even know if they had planned to make the Xbox version. Sometimes they would play those tricks. But I was pretty sure that they would make it if we didn’t have a deal.”
“We really weren’t sure whether [Xbox] was going to do anything”
-Kelly Sumner, Former Take-Two CEO
However, the deal was only for Europe as that was Deering’s jurisdiction. Sumner wanted a global deal. After all, it didn’t make sense to create an Xbox version only for the US market.
“I ran it through the system up to the Tokyo people, back to the US,” Deering explained.
“And they didn’t want to know. They were not third-party-oriented. [To them], third-party publishers and developers were, most of the time, a pain. They were always complaining and competing for the production capacity with the home studios.
“But part of the reason that we were so friendly to third parties is we didn’t really have that many home studios. In Europe we had Psygnosis and a few partnerships. But that was it.”
However, PlayStation Japan was very interested, and Tokyo pressured the US team to sign the game.
“The States were really dragging their feet,” Sumner added. “They didn’t get it. Chris and the guys at Sony in the UK absolutely got the game, but the guys in the US didn’t. And they somewhat got dragged along.”
Check out the full chats with Deering and Sumner in today’s The Game Business Show.

Xbox turned to its CEO to win over Rockstar
Microsoft made Rockstar a primary target when it came to its Xbox 360.
“GTA 3 changed everything,” said Peter Moore, who was oversaw the launches of Xbox 360 and Dreamcast. “We knew the cultural phenomenon that was GTA, and we had to have it on our platform.”
He continued: “We spent a year and a half visiting third parties, ‘we’ being primarily Robbie Bach, myself, George Peckham, Blake Fisher and John Smith. Our job was to convince them that we were for real this time, that we knew what we were doing, that high-speed broadband was going to be a thing, and that this was going to be a real toe-to-toe fight. We were not saying, ‘We’re going to win and PlayStation 3 will be a distant second.’ That wasn’t the narrative. It was: ‘This is going to be a milestone in the history of our industry of two very powerful companies with two very powerful platforms coming together.’
“GTA got caught up in the middle of that as the prettiest girl at the dance.”
At one point, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer was brought in to meet with the Sam and Dan Houser at E3.
“The details of that meeting will stay forever in the vault,” Moore said.
It worked. At E3 2006, Moore revealed that GTA 4 would be coming to Xbox 360 via a tattoo on his arm.
“It was a big E3. I think that levelled the playing field even more for the Xbox 360 versus the impending arrival of PS3.”
But Xbox wanted more than that. GTA 4 would inevitably cause people to buy a console, and Moore wanted to make sure that console was Xbox 360. So, he sought some form of exclusivity agreement, one that required “a large check”.
“It was very difficult for third parties to grant an exclusive,” Moore said. “This was going to be two nose-to-nose, toe-to-toe consoles for this cycle, and so a third-party developer giving one of their titles exclusively meant they were probably missing out on [hundreds of millions of dollars].
“So, you negotiated for what edge could you get, and so having downloadable content that was exclusive to your platform, time-based or permanently exclusive, was where you went in those days. And that was enough, at times, to tip the scales for a consumer who was considering: ‘Do I buy an Xbox 360 or a PlayStation 3?’ If they were a real aficionado of Grand Theft Auto, and had to play the DLC, that was a scale-tipper towards us.”
Xbox signed a temporary deal for 2009 expansions The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony. This partnership, and a deal with Nintendo for the DS game Chinatown Wars, remain the only times that GTA partnered with a non-PlayStation console.
Three other fun facts from today’s Show:

It said the claimant failed to argue that pricing was unfair, and that PlayStation operates in a ‘systems market’ and is not a monopoly.
Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis has seen further job losses, with 60 employees – around a third of the company – made redundant. Studio head Heather Hazen has left the studio.
GTA 6 has been nominated for eight aways in The Game Awards, including Game of the Year. The Rockstar title will face off against 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Resident Evil Requiem, Phantom Blade Zero, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake in the headline category. The event this year will be streamed via over 40 platforms, including Disney Plus and Roblox.
Unity has launched a fellowship program where indie developers planning to launch a game within the next year can get a $50,000 grant with no equity or repayment. Ten studios will be selected for the grant, with the recipients announced at GDC in March 2027. The teams will also feature advice from experts on PR and publishing, and will be connected with publishers.
Sticking with Unity, the firm has acquired Synty Studios, a publisher of 3D art packs for game developers. The art will be integrate into Unity Spark, the company’s AI-native game creation platform.
Paradox Interactive CEO Fredrik Wester will step down from his role on January 4, 2026, to be replaced by deputy CEO Mattias Lilja.
Lego Digital Play has acquired ForthStar Games, the new studio formed by Playdemic co-founders Paul Gouge and Alex Rigby.
Mario and Zelda creator Shigeru Miyamoto will receive the first Legend Award at the 30th Annual DICE Awards next February.
That’s probably it from us this week. Enjoy GTA 6, and we’ll see you next week.

We’re joined by Kelly Sumner, Chris Deering, Shuhei Yoshida, Shawn Layden and Peter Moore to look back on the history of GTA

Christopher Dring

Listen now on Apple, Spotify or YouTube

In This Edition,

  • How Sony secured GTA 3

  • Xbox’s GTA 4 fight back

  • How GTA changed Sony’s studios

  • GTA 3’s unspent $600,000 music budget

  • Plus, GTA 6 predictions, and more stories

Hello there!

We’re out a day earlier this week for Rockstar-related reasons. And we have a fun special edition of the Show today.

The launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is an entertainment event like nothing this industry has seen before. Movies have their Star Wars moments, music have had their major album launches, and I remember Harry Potter mania vividly. But games? I think this might be a first.

GTA is about more than numbers. But we’re The Game Business, and so we’ll be watching to see if it can hit that $2 billion figure in one weekend. It’d be a remarkable feat. And I’ll be fascinated to see what happens for the artists, actors and locations that are featured within the game.

But that’s all to come. For today, I’ve decided to look back at the business history of GTA. And we have some big names sharing their insight, memories and stories from working on the business-side of GTA. We’ve got former PlayStation execs Chris Deering, Shuhei Yoshida and Shawn Layden, plus ex-Take-Two CEO Kelly Sumner and Xbox 360 boss Peter Moore. It’s a bumper edition. And you can listen to the whole thing above, or check out some of the key highlights below.

Enjoy!

PlayStation US didn’t want GTA

The exclusivity deal that brought Grand Theft Auto 3, Vice City and San Andreas to PlayStation began at E3 in Los Angeles.

“We stayed at the Sunset Marquis Hotel, which is a hotel where the British people stay,” said former PlayStation European boss Chris Deering. “The PS2 was coming, and we were thinking, ‘Well, we’re here at E3, we can make contact with major publishers and see if there’s anything we can do on exclusivity.’ Because we knew the Xbox was coming.

“We had a little meeting room. And we were visited by Kelly Sumner, who was head of Take-Two at the time.”

Deering already had his eye on a game. Before travelling to E3, he received a tip off from one of his internal third-party relations staff.

“I walked by the office and said, “Anything coming down this pipeline that’s interesting?” And someone said, ‘Well, there’s this new GTA.’ I said, ‘GTA?’ ‘Yeah. It’s really good.’

“Kelly was not the first that came through the door, but I remember it was at the end of the day. So, we didn’t have a lot of time, and he had two titles. The first one was something called State of Emergency. We took both.”

Sumner remembered: “Sony came to us and said that we were looking for a product to become exclusive, because they wanted to fend off Microsoft.

“The whole of Take-Two and Rockstar were massively supportive of PlayStation, and not massively supportive of Xbox at the time. We really weren’t sure whether [Xbox] was going to do anything. So, we were very happy to do an exclusive, but not only that, they gave us a substantial amount of cash, and for us that was pretty important. But even more important, as it turned out, was they gave us a discount on the production costs.”

Both Deering and Sumner estimates that Sony gave them between $2.50 - $3 off per unit, and so the deal was worth “tens and tens and tens of millions of dollars” for Take-Two.

Deering continued: “I said, ‘Can we do two or three in a row?’ Because I knew they’d be another one. And it was a jovial meeting. I don’t even know if they had planned to make the Xbox version. Sometimes they would play those tricks. But I was pretty sure that they would make it if we didn’t have a deal.”

“We really weren’t sure whether [Xbox] was going to do anything”
-Kelly Sumner, Former Take-Two CEO

However, the deal was only for Europe as that was Deering’s jurisdiction. Sumner wanted a global deal. After all, it didn’t make sense to create an Xbox version only for the US market.

“I ran it through the system up to the Tokyo people, back to the US,” Deering explained.

“And they didn’t want to know. They were not third-party-oriented. [To them], third-party publishers and developers were, most of the time, a pain. They were always complaining and competing for the production capacity with the home studios.

“But part of the reason that we were so friendly to third parties is we didn’t really have that many home studios. In Europe we had Psygnosis and a few partnerships. But that was it.”

However, PlayStation Japan was very interested, and Tokyo pressured the US team to sign the game.

“The States were really dragging their feet,” Sumner added. “They didn’t get it. Chris and the guys at Sony in the UK absolutely got the game, but the guys in the US didn’t. And they somewhat got dragged along.”

Check out the full chats with Deering and Sumner in today’s The Game Business Show.

Xbox turned to its CEO to win over Rockstar

Microsoft made Rockstar a primary target when it came to its Xbox 360.

“GTA 3 changed everything,” said Peter Moore, who was oversaw the launches of Xbox 360 and Dreamcast. “We knew the cultural phenomenon that was GTA, and we had to have it on our platform.”

He continued: “We spent a year and a half visiting third parties, ‘we’ being primarily Robbie Bach, myself, George Peckham, Blake Fisher and John Smith. Our job was to convince them that we were for real this time, that we knew what we were doing, that high-speed broadband was going to be a thing, and that this was going to be a real toe-to-toe fight. We were not saying, ‘We’re going to win and PlayStation 3 will be a distant second.’ That wasn’t the narrative. It was: ‘This is going to be a milestone in the history of our industry of two very powerful companies with two very powerful platforms coming together.’

“GTA got caught up in the middle of that as the prettiest girl at the dance.”

At one point, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer was brought in to meet with the Sam and Dan Houser at E3.

“The details of that meeting will stay forever in the vault,” Moore said.

It worked. At E3 2006, Moore revealed that GTA 4 would be coming to Xbox 360 via a tattoo on his arm.

“It was a big E3. I think that levelled the playing field even more for the Xbox 360 versus the impending arrival of PS3.”

But Xbox wanted more than that. GTA 4 would inevitably cause people to buy a console, and Moore wanted to make sure that console was Xbox 360. So, he sought some form of exclusivity agreement, one that required “a large check”.

“It was very difficult for third parties to grant an exclusive,” Moore said. “This was going to be two nose-to-nose, toe-to-toe consoles for this cycle, and so a third-party developer giving one of their titles exclusively meant they were probably missing out on [hundreds of millions of dollars].

“So, you negotiated for what edge could you get, and so having downloadable content that was exclusive to your platform, time-based or permanently exclusive, was where you went in those days. And that was enough, at times, to tip the scales for a consumer who was considering: ‘Do I buy an Xbox 360 or a PlayStation 3?’ If they were a real aficionado of Grand Theft Auto, and had to play the DLC, that was a scale-tipper towards us.”

Xbox signed a temporary deal for 2009 expansions The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony. This partnership, and a deal with Nintendo for the DS game Chinatown Wars, remain the only times that GTA partnered with a non-PlayStation console.

Three other fun facts from today’s Show:

  1. Rockstar had a $600,000 budget for the music on GTA 3. However, the company never spent it. Kelly Sumner explained: “Terry Donovan [marketing at Rockstar] somehow got hold of this guy called Tommy Mottola, who’s still a huge name in the music industry. He was in charge of Sony at the time. Mottola literally got in a car and drove down to SoHo where we were based in New York, and Terry did a deal that we got the music for nothing. We gave them the rights for the CD, and we got the music for nothing. Not only was that a great commercial deal, but we got the content that Rockstar believed we needed to make the radio stations.”

  2. Take-Two deliberately kept supply low for GTA 3 to capitalize on the fear the game would get cancelled. “There was a lot of press that we were getting about ‘was it going to be banned’. So, we didn’t flood the market, which was traditional in those days. We kept the market really, really lean on the basis that people thought that it was going to get banned, and they had to buy it when it was available. We kept the market incredibly tight for probably about eight months, and literally people didn’t go, ‘Oh, I’ll get it next week’. It’s like, ‘I’ve got to get it,’ because we helped fuel the thought that it wouldn’t be around, and particularly in the US, it was going to be banned.”

  3. GTA 3 had a profound impact on PlayStation’s US studios, particularly those that worked on games aimed at children: Naughty Dog (Crash Bandicoot), Insomniac (Spyro) and Sucker Punch (Sly Cooper). “I clearly remember the impact that GTA 3, Vice City, and San Andreas had on the whole industry,” said former PlayStation Studios boss Shuhei Yoshida. “When we moved from PS2 to PS3, all three of these developers moved from character action to more mature-themed, realistic third-person action-adventure games. Naughty Dog did Uncharted, Insomniac did Resistance: Fall of Man and Sucker Punch did Infamous.”

You can read more stories, plus views on the launch of GTA 6, in today’s The Game Business Show above.

  • Sony has defeated a major $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit over the price of PlayStation games.   • Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis has seen further job losses, with 60 employees – around a third of the company – made redundant. Studio head Heather Hazen has left the studio.

  • GTA 6 has been nominated for eight aways in The Game Awards, including Game of the Year. AI Update Part 2: AI could still be hurting game sales, but in a less obvious way
Share:
Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Data Analysis
Published: 11/18/2026
Updated: 11/18/2026
In  Part 1 of this series where I revisit the question of AI disclosure on Steam, I showed that disclosure has gone from 15% of releases to around half in under two years. Today, I’m going back to the question that got us all that attention earlier this year: does using AI hurt sales?
A quick recap. Back in December 2025 I compared 9,879 commercial Steam releases with and without an AI disclosure and found that the AI games received roughly 53% fewer reviews in their first month; given that reviews are the best proxy for sales, that means those games sold significantly less. This was even after I accounted for developer experience, publisher backing, the type of game, and the month of release. I finished with a TLDR that "AI Is Neutral For Beginners But Problematic For Experienced Devs".
A year on I have three times the data, a better model, and a new ability to see how AI is being used in each game. In today's blog, I’m going to use this to cover the following:
The simple view: how do AI games compare on the face of it?
The careful view: what happens when I compare like with like?
A correction, because part of last year's TLDR doesn't hold up anymore.
Does it matter what you use AI for?
What kind of games are these, is it all just low-effort shovelware, and which AI games did sell?
Spoiler
This is the internet and people quote stuff without reading the full article. So just in case you do not read the full article, I’m putting this here to make sure I'm not misquoted.
Yes , the expected loss in sales is still there on the face of it; AI games receive significantly less sales. But most of the damage is already done by launch day, before anyone has played the game, and that changes what the findings mean!
Either the penalty of disclosing AI applies before launch and people refuse to support an AI game. Or, AI is the symptom of a wider problem, with people speed running development and not putting the care and attention into marketing and community building that a successful launch requires. I urge you to read to the end of the article, but if you don’t, this is the main takeaway.
As with last year, when I say "sales" I mostly mean "reviews". Only the developer knows their true sales, and review counts are the best public proxy I have. If you would like to read about how Game Oracle uses reviews to estimate sales you can check out our dedicated blog on the subject .
On the face of it, AI still appears to have a problem
After removing free-to-play games, unreleased games, and developers who publish faster than one game every six months (the same "slop" filter I used last year, which helps us identify honest commercial intent), I have 31,003 commercial games released between January 2025 and October 2026. Of those, 9,251 (30%) have an AI disclosure; this is a big jump from last year when that figure was 17.9%!
Our first finding is that a third of all AI games have no reviews at all, implying that they received little to no sales. Compare this to titles without AI disclosure, where only around 1-in-6 have no reviews.
Now, if you remember the milestone from Part 1 , I considered 1,000 sales as a healthy and realistic target for an indie release. It turns out games without an AI disclosure are about twice as likely to get to 1000 sales. The distribution of sales for the two groups are shown below.
Comparison of estimated Steam sales, for games with at least one estimated sale. Among those, the median game without an AI disclosure has sold an estimated 200 copies whereas the median game with a disclosure has sold only 71. The same pattern shows up in followers, our stand-in for wishlists: the median AI game has 17 whereas games without any disclosed have 47. So it’s not just sales that’s impacted, but also purchase interest.
Followers per game, our proxy for wishlists. The median game with an AI disclosure has 17 followers, against 47 for games without one. But what about player reception?
Looking only at games with at least 100 reviews, so the scores mean something, the median share of positive reviews is 82.0% for AI games and 87.1% for games without an AI disclosure. Last year this was 84.6% vs 88.3%, so proportionally it hasn’t changed that much.
Player ratings for games with at least 100 reviews. The median AI game sits at 82% positive, five points below the 87% for games without an AI disclosure. Enjoying this article? Sign up to our newsletter for monthly market insights and the
latest indie innovations

“But AI games are newer!”
If you were about to shout this at your screen, good. You're right.
AI disclosure has grown so quickly that AI games are much younger: the median AI game in our data has been on sale for 149 days whereas the median non-AI game has been on sale for around 300 days. Younger games have had less time to collect reviews. The simplest fix is to compare games released in the same quarter:
Comparing games released in the same quarter, so they are the same age. Games with an AI disclosure have a lower median review count and are less likely to reach 1,000 estimated sales in all eight quarters. In every one of the eight quarters I observed, AI games have a lower median review count and are less likely to reach 1,000 sales. Games from early 2025 have had well over a year to find their audience, and the AI ones still sit at half the median reviews of their non-AI counterparts.
So using AI is, at the very least, still correlated with poorer performance on Steam. I want to emphasize a word there: correlated . Correlation does not mean causation!
We can go deeper (again)
Correlation is where last year's analysis started, so I wanted to do the same here. But correlation doesn’t answer the most critical question: does AI disclosure impact sales?
There is a lot to account for if I'm to answer this question. AI games are not just newer. They are also more likely to be a first release and less likely to have a publisher. 76% of AI games are a first release vs 68% of games with no AI disclosure and 14% of games disclosing AI use have a publisher vs 22% of games without an AI disclosure.
This, along with countless other reasons, could explain the loss of reviews without AI having anything to do with it.
So, like in last year’s analysis, I built a statistical model to ask a much more specific question:
For the same type of game, released in the same month, on sale for the same number of days, with the same publisher backing and the same developer experience, how many reviews does a game with an AI disclosure get compared to one without?
The ingredients come from last year's causal diagram (the one that made it look like I'd had a mental break). However, three things have changed:
I count all reviews to date, not just the first month , and account for how long each game has been on sale using a correction term within the model itself.
I count reviews from Steam purchases, not keys bought elsewhere. Although I did check, and re-running on all reviews makes almost no difference.
The model is different. Last year's model, and three close relatives, could not reproduce what Steam review counts actually look like: a huge pile of games with nothing, and a tiny number of hits with everything. The new model treats "does this game get any reviews?" and "how many?" as two separate questions. It is fundamentally a more robust model compared to last year.
The Results
Take two developers making the same type of game, releasing in the same month, with the same publisher status and the same level of experience. The one with the AI disclosure can expect 49% fewer reviews. If developer A got 100 reviews, developer B, who made a similar game but disclosed AI, would get about 50.
Last year's result next to this year's. The average expected loss in reviews is now 63%, and for a typical game it is 49%: about half the reviews.
Hang on, why are there two numbers this year?
Because averages on Steam are a bit misleading. The top 1% of games hold 76% of all reviews, so an "average" is mostly a statement about the top hits.
Most of you aren't asking "what happens to the whole market?". You're asking "what happens to a game like mine?". So the model also reports the expected reduction in reviews for a typical game, the middle of the pack among games that get reviewed. To simplify things, going forward I will just discuss the expected reduction in reviews/sales for a typical game that discloses AI use compared to a typical game that does not, but I wanted to show both for transparency.
In that cohort, games with AI disclosures get 49.5% fewer reviews; so about half the reviews of a game without a disclosure. The chance of getting any reviews at all also drops, from 82.4% to 74.4%.
So far, then: compared on the things last year’s model controlled for, a typical AI game gets about half the reviews, and that barely moves across the robustness checks.
However! This is the difference between games that are comparable to the things I controlled for in last year's analysis! Later on I find something it doesn't control for and this thing accounts for most of the effect! So please don't stop reading at 49.5%!
I tried to break the model
Any good scientist knows that you should try and break things before you make your mind up. A single number from a single model deserves suspicion, so I re-ran the analysis a bunch of different ways:
The main result and eleven attempts to break it. The expected loss of reviews for a typical game stays between 46% and 50%. Each of the results above is like running the model in a different hypothetical world with different inputs. A number of interesting scenarios here are worth discussing:
First-month reviews only, like last year: we would expect a 46% reduction in reviews, fitted on 26,745 games. So our result isn't an artefact of counting reviews to date.
Matching on store-page content (the embeddings behind our Steam Map): the loss of reviews barely shifts for the typical game. So the type of game being made accounts for little of it.
Leaving out early-access graduates. Games like Valheim and Palworld left early access in 2026, so Steam lists them as 2026 releases but there are years of reviews behind them; I wanted to make sure this wasn’t skewing things and the results suggest it isn’t.
None of the scenarios I ran came anywhere close to zero effect on sales. But, none of these scenarios account for how prepared a game was on launch day either. I’ll discuss that soon, and it turns out it matters a lot!
The full list of checks that I did are in the methodology at the bottom of the article.
But what about skill, talent, marketing, and just plain old luck?
I need to provide the same caveat as last year, and just like last year, it's a big one. Even though I would love to, I simply can't measure how skilled a team is, how much money they have, or how good their marketing is. If the developers who reach for AI also tend to have less of all three, then some of this reduction in reviews and sales is "under-resourced teams sell less" and not "AI games sell less".
Last year I tackled this by imagining an unmeasured "X-factor". I came up with hypothetical scenarios of how strongly this unmeasured factor is tied to using AI and how much it moves reviews, then saw what was left of the AI effect. This is called a sensitivity analysis.
Last year, an X-factor that nearly tripled the odds of using AI and cut reviews by 22% was enough to wipe out the penalty for AI disclosure. In other words, some unmeasured variable (e.g. marketing or skill) could account for the difference in sales.
This year, the same X-factor barely makes a dent. A typical AI game gets 49.5% fewer reviews than a comparable non-AI game. Allow for the X-factor and it still gets 46% fewer. That X-factor explains about 3 of those 49.5 points.
So how big would an X-factor need to be to explain the whole thing? A hidden factor can never explain a bigger gap than its own effect on reviews. So even in the most extreme case, where every AI developer has it and no other developer does, it would have to halve a game's reviews all on its own. That's as big as the AI effect itself. If it's any less tied to AI use, it would have to be bigger still. That's enormous.
I want you to hold onto this thought though, because further down I go looking for something that big, and I may have just found it. But first, a correction…
A correction: The Impact of using AI is not "neutral for beginners"
This is the part where I have to hold my hands up and apologise.
Last year, I read that heatmap from the sensitivity analysis as two stories: an inexperienced developer whose game was going to struggle anyway, for whom AI makes no difference, and an experienced studio that gets hammered for using it.
The problem is that the heatmap can't tell you that. Each cell answers "what would the AI effect be for everyone if this hidden factor existed?". The rows are not types of developer. Ultimately, what I did was read a chart about what I don't know as if it were a chart about who the developers are.
This year I tested the impact of prior experience directly instead. I did this by letting the model estimate a different AI effect depending on how many games a developer has released before:
Reviews for a typical game with and without an AI disclosure, by how many games the developer has released before. Everyone loses about half their reviews or more, and the share lost grows a little with experience, from 47% for a first release to 59% for developers with three or more. The impact of using AI is not neutral for beginners. A first-time developer creating a typical game with an AI disclosure gets about 47% fewer reviews, and is 8 percentage points less likely to get any reviews at all.
Experienced developers do have more to lose, just not in the way I said. For a typical game, the loss actually grows a little with experience: 47% fewer reviews for a first release, 54% for developers with one or two previous games, and 59% for three or more (partly because a first release starts so low that it has less room to fall). And because experienced developers start from a higher base, the number of reviews lost grows much faster. A typical first release would get about 8 or 9 reviews without a disclosure and 4 or 5 with one, so it loses about 4. A typical game from a developer with three or more previous releases would get about 44 without and 18 with, so it loses about 26. The proportional hit is a bit bigger for experienced developers, but the number of reviews (and sales) lost is wildly different.
So the honest version of last year's TLDR would have been: everyone takes a big hit, beginners included; experienced developers lose a slightly bigger share, and because they start from more, it costs them far more.
Quick note: “previous releases" is not a measure of talent or budget. It is just the best proxy I have for developer experience, and it's still a rough one, so please take that into account when reading these statistics.
New this year: does it matter how you use AI?
Last year I wrote that I couldn't include how AI is used, and that it matters.
Thanks to the disclosure classifier I built for Part 1 , this year I can at least look at what AI was used for, comparing games disclosing each use against games with no disclosure at all:
The reduction in review count broken down by what the AI disclosure says AI was used for. Every category sits below zero; localisation and voice have the smallest expected loss of reviews and the widest uncertainty. Every category comes with fewer reviews overall. The smallest losses in expected sales are for localisation (25%) and voice (40%), though even for localisation the loss stays clear of zero. My best guess is that translating a game with AI is the one use here that plausibly brings more players through the door, and it sits on top of a finished game rather than replacing part of it. But that is a guess.
The largest expected loss is for AI-written code (67%), which really surprised me, since my assumption was that AI generated art drives the most negative discourse around AI in games. But, before anyone uses that to win an argument online: the categories overlap heavily (a game disclosing AI code usually discloses AI art and music too), the labels come from a classifier reading free text, and plenty of developers use coding assistants without ever mentioning it.
So what kind of games are these, anyway?
Whenever I talk about this analysis, somebody says: "Well, obviously. AI games are all asset flips and incremental-game or friendslop shovelware. Of course they don't sell."
That's really two claims. One, that AI games pile into a particular corner of Steam. Two, that they're a flood of low-effort releases that were never going to sell, AI or no AI. Luckily, both are testable, at least partly.
Are AI games flooding one genre?
Maybe, but not to the extent people believe. Every one of Steam's genres sits between 25% and 35% AI, against 30% disclosing AI overall. The player-applied tags show more variation: AI disclosure runs at 40% to 45% in text-based games, card games, tabletop and management sims, and under 20% in platformers and hand-drawn games. That makes sense to be honest, the top of the list is games made largely of still images and text, which is what today's AI tools produce most easily.
The most detailed view comes from our Steam Map , which places every game on Steam according to its store page content, and groups them into a few hundred segments of similar games:
The Game Oracle Steam Map, with each market segment shaded by the share of its games that disclose AI. The lighter areas are the most AI-heavy segments: football and sports management, jigsaw puzzles, shop simulators, card games, visual novels and board games. Most of the map is the same mid-red. Half of all market segments are between 23% and 34% AI, and AI games are the majority in just 8 of them, which account for  2% of all AI games on Steam. That small, bright island at the bottom left is jigsaw puzzles: 22 of its 40 games disclose AI, which also makes sense when the whole game is a set of pictures.
Is it just that those genres sell badly?
Maybe card battlers and visual novels are simply crowded, low-selling corners of Steam, right? To test this, I compared AI games with non-AI games from the same market segment, released in the same quarter. It barely changes anything: 12% of AI games reach 1,000 sales, against 24% of all non-AI games and 23% of non-AI games matched to them on market segment and release quarter. In 107 of the 111 segments with enough games to compare, AI games do worse than non-AI games in the same market segment.
So genre isn't the explanation. Whatever is going on with the impact of using AI happens within all genres.
A flood of games nobody was waiting for?
That leaves the second claim, which I find much harder to dismiss: that AI has made it cheap to finish a game, so we’re seeing a wave of games shipped quickly, without the months of wishlist-building, community work, and polish that a successful launch normally needs.
I can't measure effort, but I can measure some things that tend to come along with effort. AI games are a bit more likely to be a developer’s first game, a bit less likely to have a publisher or a demo, and support more languages. The typical AI game had its store page up for 52 days before release whereas the typical non-AI game had theirs up for 167 days. More than half of AI games launched within two months of their page going live. This also shows up in the audience they built as well: the typical AI game goes into launch day with 6 followers, versus a median of 20 followers for non-AI games.

Finally, I asked the model to control for both together, which is the fairest approach. This model reported the reduction in reviews as 16% for a typical game. So the impact of AI disclosure is smaller, but not zero.
But why does adding the store-page runway on top of followers make the reduction in expected reviews a little bigger?
Among games with the same following on launch day, the ones that built their following quickly go on to sell better (a fast-growing audience is a good sign), and AI games are much more likely to have gathered their followers quickly. When I looked at followers alone, it appears that AI games were quietly getting credit for this rapid accumulation effect.
So here's where that leaves the “X-factor” I spoke about earlier: I said its effect would need to be enormous to explain the reduction in reviews. This right here is what an enormous effect looks like! The size of the  audience a game has built by launch day is one of the strongest predictors of sales anyone can have, and according to the data AI games arrive with a fraction of the audience size that is needed!
I must admit though, this isn't quite the whole story. Among games that launched with a real following, 100 followers or more, the typical AI game still ends up with about 12% fewer reviews than a non-AI game that started with the same audience. But that is a very different number from the 49% reduction in reviews we saw at the beginning of this analysis!
Two ways to read this
I want to be careful here, because this result can be made to say two very different things.
It was never really about AI. AI tools have made it possible to get a game onto Steam faster and cheaper than ever. A lot of the games doing that are first projects, released  with a few weeks' notice, no demo, no publisher, and no audience. Games like that have always struggled on Steam. They did not sink because they use (and disclose) AI, it's just what a lot of them have in common.
The penalty of disclosing AI arrives before launch. Followers result from players looking at a store page and deciding they care about the game being made. The AI disclosure is on that page from day one, and so, usually, is the AI art. If players are scrolling past it because they’re put off by AI use, a low follower count on launch day isn't an alternative explanation for the AI penalty, it is because of the use of AI that a game has a low follower count to begin with. This is essentially the same AI penalty I warned about in our original 2025 analysis, but it is just showing up before launch rather than after.
Honestly, I can't tell you which explanation is right. Personally, I suspect both are right, and they’re mixed in a way I can't measure. The short runway really has nothing to do with AI sentiment, it is a choice made by the developer. However, the low follower count could be caused by a short runway to launch and player sentiment about AI.
What I can say is narrower, and I think it’s still useful: whatever is happening to AI games has mostly happened by launch day. An AI game that does build an audience goes on to sell only a little worse than any other game with the same run-up and the same audience.
The AI games that made it
Everything above is about averages and typical games. There are of course plenty of games that are neither average nor typical. They aren't one kind of game. We’ve got a blockbuster shooter, a football game, a life sim, a live-action story game, a cosy tidying game, and a pixel-art roguelite. There is a big mix of genres here.
In most of them, AI is used for small, specific things: some paintings on a wall, a translation, placeholder voices, four assets, or one percent of the runtime, and the developers go out of their way to tell you exactly how small.
Some of them are just simply big games. Embark, Pearl Abyss and EA were going to sell games whatever their store page said.
They took their time. The median store-page runway for an AI game that passed 10,000 sales is 359 days. For those that sold under 1,000 the runway is 43 days
Another thing: BidKing is in that table with three quarters of a million copies sold but it was priced at $2.99 with AI-generated art and has a 32% positive rating. A game can sell and still not be liked.
None of this proves that careful, limited AI use is why these games sold; I picked them because they sold. But it proves the narrower point: an AI disclosure doesn't rule out a hit, and the AI games that do well look a lot like any other game that does well.
What about a first-time dev who leaned on AI?
A fair criticism of the table above is that it is made up of mostly big studios and games where AI was a footnote. So I went looking for the opposite: a developer's first game on Steam, no publisher, a disclosure that says AI did real work, and sales well above normal for its release quarter.
"Well above normal" here means at least three times the median estimated sales of every game released in the same quarter. That sounds higher than it is, since the median game sells somewhere between 15 and 110 copies.
Among first releases from self-published developers, 21% of AI games clear that bar, compared to 30% of non-AI games. Narrow it to AI games whose disclosure covers at least two kinds of in-game content, and 19% still clear it. These games are harder to find, but not exactly rare. Furthermore, it turns out 38 of those AI games have passed 10,000 estimated sales.

These games sold roughly 200 to 700 times more copies than a  typical game in their release quarter. None of them were a “mega-hit”, but every one is a first game from a self-published developer, and every one is well-reviewed.
They don't all fit the launch-day story either. Settlements Rising had its Steam store page up for well over a year and launched with about 4,500 followers: the textbook run-up with strong consistent marketing. However, Tasty Chef put their store page up only five weeks before launch  and only had around 250 followers.
One more for the exceptions pile that didn’t make the table: Dub Together, a $4.99 party game with AI-generated character art, launched two weeks after its page went up, with 12 followers, and has sold an estimated 50,000 copies.
I found these by looking for them, and a handful of exceptions doesn't change an average. But "a first-time, self-published developer who used AI for most of their art and still found an audience" is a thing that happens, and it happens more often than the loudest corners of the internet would have you believe.
So, what does this actually tell us?
What the data supports:
Games with an AI disclosure get far fewer reviews than games that are comparable on experience, publisher, genre and timing: about half as many reviews for a typical AI game and this has been the case for nearly two years, across 31,003 games, and holds up to every way I could think of to break it.
The effect of AI disclosure on reviews (and therefore sales) isn't only a beginner problem, it shows up for every kind of AI use I could measure, and it isn't a genre problem either.
Most of the effect that results in the reduction in reviews is already in place on launch day. AI games go live after a much shorter run-up and with a much smaller following. When I account for the run-up, the expected reduction in reviews for a typical game falls from 49% to 29%, and when I account for the run-up and the audience on launch day together it falls to about 16%.
An AI disclosure doesn't rule out success, including for first-time developers.
What it can't tell you:
That AI causes the drop. This is a comparison of games that exist, not an experiment. The amount of time a store page has been up before launch and the number of followers accumulated prior to launch show how much an unmeasured factor can move the expected reduction in reviews, but skill, budget and marketing effort are still mostly unmeasured.
Why the reduction in reviews happens. Last year I wrote that the "AI Stigma" is real and severely punishes developers. I was far too quick to make this claim. A wave of quickly made and lightly marketed games would leave almost the same fingerprints in this data. Personally, I think both things are happening at the same time.
Who actually used AI. I can only see who filled in the disclosure box. Games that used AI and kept quiet are sitting in the "no AI" group.
The actual sales a game has accumulated. I can only measure reviews and then estimate sales. If people who buy AI games simply review less often, that would also explain the reduction in reviews seen for AI games.
One thing I'm deliberately not making a fuss about is that the reduction in reviews looks more severe for games released from May 2026 onwards. It's tempting to write "the backlash is growing", but those games are young and their review counts are still settling. Ask me again in six months.
TLDR: the reduction in sales is real, but it is not a verdict on AI
In reality, the dust has not settled on the debate of what AI means for the games industry. If you're sceptical of AI in games, this data tells you that games disclosing AI are reaching a smaller audience in every genre and for every kind of use, and about half for a typical game, two years running. You might also conclude that players are quietly declining to follow games with an AI disclosure.
If you're enthusiastic about AI in games, then you might read this and think the reduction in reviews/sales we’ve seen is not simply a judgement handed down after launch. Rather, the reduction is explained away by how long a developer spent gathering an audience towards release, and AI games that put time into marketing and community building see different outcomes.
And if, like most developers I talk to, you're somewhere in the middle, then I don't think this analysis tells you whether to use AI or not. I think it tells you that the label on your store page matters a great deal less than what you've built by the day you press the release button. The games that struggle here are overwhelmingly games that arrive quickly and quietly. That was a losing strategy on Steam long before generative AI existed.
Approach AI with caution, use it gracefully, and give your game the run-up to launch it deserves.
In Part 3 I'll be looking at a question I never thought I would have to ask: how worried should you be about your game being cloned by AI? See you in the next one.
Methodology (for the nerds)
If you want to know exactly which games I analysed, what the model does, which checks passed and failed, and which rules I changed, it's all here.
The Data
This analysis uses the Game Oracle Steam catalogue, frozen on 7 November 2026: 31,003 paid games released between January 2025 and October 2026. Of these, 9,251 (30%) have an AI disclosure.
I excluded free-to-play games, games priced above $100, and developers whose previous releases averaged less than six months apart. This is the same rapid-release filter used last year. I checked, and restoring the last two groups makes little difference to the result.
The main outcome is review count, primarily from Steam purchases, although some records use total reviews. Games with zero reviews stay in the analysis. Estimated sales are derived from reviews, so they provide an alternative measure, not independent evidence.
“AI” means the game had an AI disclosure at the snapshot date, not necessarily at launch. Likewise, followers in the opening section are current followers.
Log-scale charts omit zero values and report their share separately. Table medians include all games.
Historical data and last year’s comparison
Rechecking last year’s release window produces broadly similar patterns, though catalogue coverage and some measurements have changed. Last year’s 53% headline and this year’s 63% are not directly comparable: the model has changed, and this year’s main outcome is reviews to date rather than first-month reviews.
What the model measures
The model adjusts for:
Developer experience, measured by previous Steam releases.
Publisher backing.
Steam genres.
Release month and time on sale.
Differences between developers with multiple games in the dataset.
Price, ratings and followers are deliberately excluded from the main adjustment. They may themselves be affected by AI use or players’ reactions to it; controlling for them could remove part of the relationship I want to measure.
The model has two parts: whether a game gets any reviews, and how many it gets if it does. A log-normal distribution accommodates the large differences between ordinary releases and Steam’s biggest hits.
For the headline comparison, the model predicts every game twice, with and without an AI disclosure, while holding all other measured characteristics constant.

These are adjusted comparisons, but I must stress they are not proof that AI causes the effect.
Model selection and fit
The four originally planned models struggled to reproduce Steam’s combination of many zero-review games and a few enormous hits. The final model was added after my tests and performed substantially better, although it still slightly underpredicts the largest non-AI hits.
The acceptance threshold and one developer-level convergence criterion were relaxed after inspecting model performance; since it is the sales performance for a typical game that is most interesting I was less concerned about poorer performance for predicting the sales of non-AI hits.
These changes concerned model assessment, not the AI-effect specification. Across all five models, the estimated average reduction ranged from 56% to 63%.
Robustness checks
Twenty of the 22 planned variations passed their quality checks. Across them, the average reduction ranged from 53% to 72%, and the typical-game review reduction from 46% to 50%.

The first-month result was also similar using only our own snapshots. Content matching narrowed the observed reduction in reviews, suggesting that differences in the kinds of games being made account for some of the association. Because it uses current store-page content, it may also absorb consequences of AI use.
The two remaining planned checks were not relied on: the earlier-release-only model failed its quality checks, and the independently verified review-source subset was too small.
An additional, unplanned check excluded 2,013 games with reviews predating their listed release date, consistent with earlier early-access launches. These games account for 27% of reviews. Removing them narrowed the average reduction in reviews to 59%, while the difference for a typical-game remained about 49%.
Unmeasured differences
The “X-factor” sensitivity tests show how a hypothetical unmeasured factor could change the result. Under its assumptions, removing the reduction in reviews entirely would require a factor that both sharply reduces reviews and is almost confined to AI-disclosing developers. This is a sensitivity exercise, not evidence that unmeasured differences are absent.
This year’s analysis is a fresh calculation and not a directly comparable update of last year’s. A separate scenario assuming some undisclosed AI use did widen the estimated reduction in reviews, but that result depends on the assumed pattern of non-disclosure and I just can’t reliably justify that analysis.
Experience and types of AI use
For the average game, there is no clear evidence that developer experience changes the AI association with review counts. For a typical game, the reduction grows with experience: 47% for first releases, 54% for one or two previous releases and 59% for three or more (the 12-point gap between first releases and three or more has a 95% credible interval of 1.5 to 21 points). The reduction in the chance of receiving any reviews is similar across groups: about eight percentage points for first releases and seven for developers with three or more previous releases.
Previous releases measure experience on Steam, not skill, resources or budget. Seventy per cent of games in the dataset are first releases.
AI-use categories come from a classifier reading store-page disclosures. Each category is compared with games without a disclosure, using the same model. Three limitations in this classification model matter:
Categories overlap: a game may disclose art, code and music together, so category estimates cannot isolate or rank their individual effects.
Labels describe disclosed use, not an inspection of development files. Removing uncertain classifications changed no category’s average estimate by more than about ten percentage points.
Undisclosed use remains invisible, particularly for coding assistants.
Live-generated content was excluded from category comparisons because only 85 games disclosed it.
Game types and the Steam Map
AI disclosure appears across the market: between 25% and 35% of games in each Steam genre. It is more common in text-based games, card games, tabletop games and management-related tags, and less common in platformers and hand-drawn games.
AI disclosure appears across every Steam genre, ranging from 25% in adventure and racing to 35% in simulation and strategy, against 30% overall. Player-applied tags reveal more variation: 45% of text-based games disclose AI use, compared with 16% of hand-drawn games. Games tagged “Artificial Intelligence” have the highest disclosure rate at 66%, while those tagged “LGBTQ+” have the lowest at 11%. The Steam Map groups games into market segments using their store text and images. Among segments with at least 100 games, AI disclosure ranges from 12% to 60%, although most sit much closer to the overall 30% share. AI games are a majority in only eight segments, containing under 2% of all AI games.
The outcome also appears within market segments: in 107 of 111 sufficiently large, mixed segments, a smaller share of AI-disclosing games reaches 1,000 estimated sales.
Even within the same Steam Map neighbourhood of similar games, titles disclosing AI use are generally less likely to reach 1,000 estimated sales. The gap appears across neighbourhoods with both low and high rates of AI disclosure.
These comparisons describe where AI games sit in the market but they do not establish why their outcomes differ.

Comparing games with similar launch positions
Simple comparisons match the groups within release quarters on Steam Map market segment, runway or launch-day following. Among games launching with at least 100 followers, the median AI game has 68 reviews against 77 for matched non-AI games; 63% versus 65% reach 1,000 estimated sales.

It just so happens that AI games are more concentrated among this group.
These runs locate much of the difference in games’ position at launch. They do not explain its cause. If AI changes development time or discourages players from following, adjusting for runway or followers removes part of that effect.
What my study does, and doesn’t, show
Games that disclose AI use receive substantially fewer reviews than games without a disclosure, even after adjusting for several measured differences. The pattern persists across alternative analyses, but narrows sharply when comparing games with similar launch-day followings.
The study does not establish that AI causes the reduction in reviews, distinguish production choices from audience reactions, or measure skill, budget and marketing directly. It measures disclosed AI use, not all AI use, and review-based outcomes, not independently observed sales.

AI Update Part 2: AI could still be hurting game sales, but in a less obvious way

Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Data Analysis

In Part 1 of this series where I revisit the question of AI disclosure on Steam, I showed that disclosure has gone from 15% of releases to around half in under two years. Today, I’m going back to the question that got us all that attention earlier this year: does using AI hurt sales?

A quick recap. Back in December 2025 I compared 9,879 commercial Steam releases with and without an AI disclosure and found that the AI games received roughly 53% fewer reviews in their first month; given that reviews are the best proxy for sales, that means those games sold significantly less. This was even after I accounted for developer experience, publisher backing, the type of game, and the month of release. I finished with a TLDR that "AI Is Neutral For Beginners But Problematic For Experienced Devs".

A year on I have three times the data, a better model, and a new ability to see how AI is being used in each game. In today's blog, I’m going to use this to cover the following:

  1. The simple view: how do AI games compare on the face of it?

  2. The careful view: what happens when I compare like with like?

  3. A correction, because part of last year's TLDR doesn't hold up anymore.

  4. Does it matter what you use AI for?

  5. What kind of games are these, is it all just low-effort shovelware, and which AI games did sell?

Spoiler

This is the internet and people quote stuff without reading the full article. So just in case you do not read the full article, I’m putting this here to make sure I'm not misquoted. 

Yes, the expected loss in sales is still there on the face of it; AI games receive significantly less sales. But most of the damage is already done by launch day, before anyone has played the game, and that changes what the findings mean! 

Either the penalty of disclosing AI applies before launch and people refuse to support an AI game. Or, AI is the symptom of a wider problem, with people speed running development and not putting the care and attention into marketing and community building that a successful launch requires. I urge you to read to the end of the article, but if you don’t, this is the main takeaway.

As with last year, when I say "sales" I mostly mean "reviews". Only the developer knows their true sales, and review counts are the best public proxy I have. If you would like to read about how Game Oracle uses reviews to estimate sales you can check out our dedicated blog on the subject.

On the face of it, AI still appears to have a problem

After removing free-to-play games, unreleased games, and developers who publish faster than one game every six months (the same "slop" filter I used last year, which helps us identify honest commercial intent), I have 31,003 commercial games released between January 2025 and October 2026. Of those, 9,251 (30%) have an AI disclosure; this is a big jump from last year when that figure was 17.9%!

Our first finding is that a third of all AI games have no reviews at all, implying that they received little to no sales. Compare this to titles without AI disclosure, where only around 1-in-6 have no reviews. 

Now, if you remember the milestone from Part 1, I considered 1,000 sales as a healthy and realistic target for an indie release. It turns out games without an AI disclosure are about twice as likely to get to 1000 sales. The distribution of sales for the two groups are shown below.

The same pattern shows up in followers, our stand-in for wishlists: the median AI game has 17 whereas games without any disclosed have 47. So it’s not just sales that’s impacted, but also purchase interest.

But what about player reception? 

Looking only at games with at least 100 reviews, so the scores mean something, the median share of positive reviews is 82.0% for AI games and 87.1% for games without an AI disclosure. Last year this was 84.6% vs 88.3%, so proportionally it hasn’t changed that much.
